result:
There's a particular kind of quiet that settles over a city just before dawn. The traffic has thinned, the night-shift workers have drifted home, and even the birds seem to hesitate before committing to the day. I love that hour. Not for any dramatic reason—it's just when the world feels most honest, stripped of the performance that daylight demands.

Lately, I've been thinking about how much of life happens in the in-between spaces. The pause before answering a question. The walk from one room to another. The few seconds after closing a book but before opening the next. These are the moments that don't get photographed or posted, and yet they might be where the actual living occurs. We're so focused on milestones—births, promotions, weddings, retirements—that we forget the connective tissue. The ordinary Tuesdays. The unmemorable meals. The conversations that don't go anywhere in particular but somehow leave you feeling less alone.

I wonder if we'll look back on this era and wish we'd been less efficient, less optimized, less determined to extract productivity from every waking minute. There used to be a word for it—leisure, maybe, though that word has been colonized by its opposite. The Greeks had a better term: *scholé*, from which we get "school," but which originally meant simply "free time." Not empty time. Not wasted time. Just time that belongs to you, unencumbered by obligation or outcome.

Maybe that's what I'm really trying to say: not every moment needs a point. Some moments are their own reward, and recognizing that might be the most radical act available to us.

The birds are starting now. The day is arriving whether I'm ready or not. But I had my quiet hour, and that feels like enough.
